meta.description: Words, phrases, and constructions that statistical detectors and human readers associate with machine generation. Removing or replacing them is necessary hygiene; the structural and discourse layers carry more of the signal.
meta.application_rule: Replace contextually; the substitute depends on what the sentence means. Do not replace every instance; leave some formal words standing where they fit. Uniform replacement is itself a signal. This contextual, leave-some-standing rule is Tier-2 and applies to flagged words/phrases only. It never applies to Tier-1 prohibitions (em-dashes, banned structures); see foundation.enforcement.
meta.usage: First pass of the application protocol. Call humanizer_get_lexical_patterns(risk_level=...) to filter by severity. Apply the application_rule above for every substitution decision.
meta.research_basis: Drawn from Przystalski et al. (2024) SHAP analysis, Grammarly common AI words corpus, Terčon & Dobrovoljc (2025) survey of 44 studies, and Wikipedia AI writing guidelines.

flagged_verbs.notes: One of the most-cited AI tells. Almost never used in natural human prose.
Travel-brochure register ('nestled in the heart of the valley'). Sibling of 'bustling' and 'hidden gem'.
Almost always replaceable with 'use' with no loss of meaning.
One of the strongest single-word AI tells in the post-ChatGPT scientific corpus. The bare verb is distinct from the flagged transition 'This underscores the importance of'.
flagged_verbs.research_basis: Kobak et al., Science Advances 2025 (doi:10.1126/sciadv.adt3813): excess frequency ratio r=13.8. Juzek & Ward, COLING 2025: +904% in PubMed abstracts 2020-2024.
Juzek & Ward, COLING 2025 (arXiv:2412.11385): 'surpassing' +667% in PubMed abstracts 2020-2024.

Especially 'embark on a journey'. Pairs with the flagged noun 'journey'.
'Resonate with' is near-universal in AI marketing copy.
Orwell rule 2. Officialese rather than AI register, and there is no context where 'start' will not do.

One of the most statistically overrepresented AI adjectives.

flagged_qualifiers.description: AI-generated writing plays it safe by using hedging phrases that soften statements. While some hedging is natural, AI overuses it uniformly. Human writers hedge selectively: firmly on some points, cautiously on others.

alternatives: Or name who holds the view, if the source names them

flagged_qualifiers.rule: Human writers commit firmly to some claims and hedge others. When rewriting, keep the source's own hedges, because each one marks how sure the writer is, and dropping it hardens the claim (absolute_rules AR-001). 'The drug probably reduces symptoms in most patients.' keeps its 'probably'. The phrases in this list are stock wordings of a limit. Where the source uses one, swap it for a plain alternative that marks the same limit, so 'Typically' becomes 'Usually'. Cut one only where it marks no limit the source states, and where several qualifiers stack on one claim, keep the one that marks the source's limit. If every paragraph carries a formulaic qualifier, the text reads as AI-generated.

vocabulary_diversity.description: The direction of whole-text lexical diversity is model-dependent, so it is not a reliable tell and this server does not measure it. AI text does recycle the same distinctive expressions and generic nouns across a piece (the flagged lexicon, the stock frames in banned_structures) and favors the expected word over the one the context calls for, so look for a marked expression that repeats.
vocabulary_diversity.history: Corrected 2026-10-30. Herbold et al. (2023) found ChatGPT essays MORE lexically diverse than student essays, and Kendro, Maloney and Jarvis (2025) found newer models more diverse than older ones while still reading as less human.

metrics.ttr: Type-Token Ratio. Not a usable signal: depending on the model, AI text scores lower, equal or higher than human text. Do not raise it by swapping in synonyms.
metrics.hapax_legomenon_rate: Proportion of words used only once. Same caveat as the type-token ratio: model-dependent, so not a target.
metrics.unique_word_count: Not a target. A passage with many unique words can still read as machine-made if the words are the expected ones.

rewriting_guidance: Use the same word for the same thing.
Replace generic nouns with specific ones: 'factors' → name the factors the source names; 'things' → name the things the source names.
Prefer the plain short word where it says the same thing.

word_length_patterns.description: AI text tends to use longer tokens and does not shorten words when context makes meaning predictable, a tendency humans naturally exhibit.
rewriting_guidance: In casual or conversational passages, prefer shorter words over longer synonyms.
Use the word the sentence needs, short or long. Do not mix lengths for effect.
Contractions follow the register and the source: use them where the source does or the register is casual, and leave them out where it is formal. Set no ratio.

nominalization.description: AI text systematically converts verbs into noun forms, producing heavier, more abstract phrasing. This nominalization pattern is a distinct structural-lexical signal beyond individual word substitution.
nominalization.ai_pattern: AI favors noun-form constructions over direct verb forms: 'the implementation of X' instead of 'we implemented X', 'the utilization of resources' instead of 'using resources'. This creates a dense, bureaucratic tone that distances the reader from the action.
nominalization.human_pattern: Human writers default to verb-driven sentences. They say 'we decided' not 'a decision was made', 'this shows' not 'this serves as a demonstration of'. Nominalizations appear in human text but are balanced by active, verb-led constructions.

rules.rule: Convert nominalizations back to verbs when the agent is known.
rules.guidance: 'The implementation of the new policy by the committee' → 'The committee implemented the new policy.' If the agent is unknown, the nominalization may be the better choice, but ask whether the agent is genuinely unknown or just being hidden.
Two or more 'the X of Y' phrases in a single sentence is a strong AI signal. 'The optimization of the utilization of resources' should become 'using resources better.'
Technical writing legitimately uses nominalizations as established terms ('risk assessment', 'load balancing'). The problem is density: three nominalizations in two sentences reads as AI.

nominalization.research_basis: Herbold et al. (2023) and Reinhart et al. (2024) both find higher nominalization rates in AI text. This overlaps with the existing POS finding that AI overuses nouns relative to verbs.

abstract_concrete_balance.description: AI defaults to abstract, intangible nouns while human writers ground claims in concrete, observable specifics.
abstract_concrete_balance.ai_pattern: AI gravitates toward words like 'framework', 'methodology', 'paradigm', 'dynamic', 'landscape', 'ecosystem': nouns that name categories rather than things you can point at.
abstract_concrete_balance.human_pattern: Human writers anchor abstract ideas in tangible language the source supplies. If the notes say classrooms and lecture halls, 'the educational landscape' becomes 'classrooms and lecture halls'. If the notes say meetings with the people who use the product, 'stakeholder engagement' becomes that. With no such detail, keep the abstract term and add none (absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: For every abstract noun, ask: can I name the concrete thing it refers to?
rules.guidance: 'Factors' → name the ones the source names. 'Challenges' → describe one the source describes. 'Stakeholders' → say who, if the source does. 'Resources' → specify which, if the source does. If the concrete version is available and no shorter than the abstract one, prefer it; if the source gives none, keep the abstract noun.

rules.rule: Name the concrete thing the source names.
rules.guidance: Concrete nouns that invoke a mental image ('spreadsheet', 'parking lot', 'whiteboard', 'inbox') anchor the reader's attention more than abstract containers ('tool', 'space', 'platform', 'system'). Use the concrete noun the source gives; swapping in one it does not give adds a fact (absolute_rules AR-001).

abstract_concrete_balance.research_basis: Opara (2025) identifies AbstractNounCount as a discriminating stylometric feature in the StyloAI framework, linked to higher-level cognitive functions in human writing.

adverb_patterns.description: AI text consistently underuses adverbs, particularly manner and degree adverbs. Where the source has them, keeping them keeps the writer's fine-grained judgments.
adverb_patterns.ai_pattern: Older and smaller models underuse degree and manner adverbs; when they do use adverbs, they tend to be generic intensifiers (significantly, effectively). The direction is model-specific for downtoners such as barely and nearly, which some models overuse and others avoid. The tell is an adverb that carries no judgment.
adverb_patterns.human_pattern: Human writers use adverbs to calibrate precision. 'It mostly works' says something different from 'it works', and the choice between them reflects a real judgment call.
adverb_patterns.human_adverbs_to_keep_notes: Keep one of these where the source already uses it, and where the source has none, add none (absolute_rules AR-001). 'quietly' (the BS-033 / AP-046 tic), 'actually' (counted by credibility_insistence) and 'honestly' (the AP-045 false-candour beat) are left off this list. A degree adverb belongs in the sentence only when it carries the writer's own assessment; adding one to look human is the same move as adding a contraction to look human.
adverb_patterns.history: Pruned 2026-10-30 because the list contradicted this server's own detectors. Reinhart et al. (PNAS 2025) found GPT-4o overusing barely and nearly while the Llama 3 models avoid them.

rules.rule: Keep the degree adverbs that calibrate a claim.
rules.guidance: Where the source says how far a claim holds ('mostly', 'barely', 'roughly'), keep that adverb, because it carries the writer's assessment. Do not add one the source lacks, since that softens or hardens the claim (absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: Keep the manner adverbs the source gives.
rules.guidance: Where the source says how something happened ('The team reluctantly responded'), keep the adverb, because the manner tells the reader something about the people involved. Do not add a manner the source does not state (absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: Let adverb density follow the source.
rules.guidance: A passage the source qualifies carefully keeps its adverbs, and a passage it states directly stays plain. Do not add or strip adverbs to change the density.

adverb_patterns.research_basis: Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024) UPOS frequency data shows ADV at 3.26% in human text vs. 2.61% in Falcon and 3.41-3.68% in LLaMA. Ardeshirifar (2025) confirms human text uses adverbs and adverbial modifiers more frequently.

credibility_insistence.description: AI-assisted writing often vouches for the authenticity of its own account by repeatedly insisting it is real, actual, genuine, or true. A human rarely needs to insist their own work is real; the insistence is a defensive credibility hedge, and the DENSITY of the token set across a document is the tell, not any single use.
credibility_insistence.ai_pattern: The same reality-asserting lemma recurs throughout a piece ('a real engagement', 'the real one', 'the design is real', 'the real flow'). Each use passes any single-token check, but the repetition reads as a writer arguing for their own credibility.
credibility_insistence.human_pattern: Human writers let the specifics carry credibility. They name the client, the constraint, the date, the artifact, and almost never label their own account 'real'. When they do, it is once, for a genuine contrast.
exclusions: one sentence-initial 'actually' as a discourse marker
rewriting_guidance: If one of these tokens appears three or more times, cut all but at most one. The narrative detail should establish that the work is real; you should not have to say so.

Replace the assertion with the specific that justified it. Where the source says 'a real engagement', give the stage it is at, such as 'a mid-build engagement'; where it says 'the real flow', name the flow.
Keep a single use only where it draws a genuine contrast (e.g. real versus hypothetical), and make that contrast explicit.
credibility_insistence.research_basis: proposed-rules PR2-#1; in-the-wild audit of nicojan.com/work/art-studio-blueprint (2026-06-28), where seven uses of 'real' in ~1,500 words passed the checker clean.

orwell.description: The plainness pass, from Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' (1946). The humanizer layers catch what marks text as machine-made, and this pass catches what makes any prose flabby. It runs after the fix rounds of the verification loop and before its last check on the assembled document, because cutting words changes rhythm and a cut is cheaper to make than to undo.
orwell.usage: The checker flags only rule 1, as banned_structures BS-041, and only over a closed list of figures. Rules 3 and 4 are judgment and live in the self_review rubric. The substitution lists below are for the calling model to apply contextually, per this layer's application_rule.

rules.text: Never use a metaphor, simile or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print.
rules.note: Mechanized over a closed list as BS-041. The list is not the class: read the piece for any image you did not choose deliberately.

rules.text: Never use a long word where a short one will do.
rules.note: Partly mechanized: the flagged_verbs and flagged_adjectives lists already carry the AI-register half (utilize, facilitate, endeavor, subsequently), and the officialese half is in long_word_substitutions below.

rules.text: If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out.
rules.note: Judgment, and the rule that does the most work in a long document. The padding_phrases list is a starting point, not the rule.

rules.text: Never use the passive where you can use the active.
rules.note: Judgment. Deliberately not mechanized: a be-plus-participle detector fires on every legitimate passive, and the legitimate ones are common in exactly the registers this server is used for (method sections, regulatory writing, anything where the agent is genuinely unknown or irrelevant).

rules.text: Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent.
rules.note: Has a carve-out. See jargon_carve_out below and caveats.jargon_substitution_loses_meaning.

rules.text: Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.
rules.note: The escape hatch, and it is real. A sentence that obeys all five and reads wrong loses.

padding_phrases.phrase: it is important to note that
padding_phrases.cut_to: cut; if it were not important it would not be in the draft
cut, or replace the adjective with a stronger one

jargon_carve_out.rule: Rule 5 does not license replacing a domain term that has no everyday equivalent. Define it in plain words at first use, then use the term plainly. Do not substitute.
jargon_carve_out.explanation: A term of art often names something no ordinary word names. Swapping 'statutory release' for 'automatic release' or 'Protected B' for 'confidential' loses the precise thing the argument depends on, and a reader who needs the argument needs the term. The failure Orwell was attacking is jargon used to avoid a plain statement, not jargon used because it is correct. So the test is: does an everyday word mean the same thing? If yes, use it. If no, define once and keep the term.
jargon_carve_out.worked_example: First use: 'statutory release, the point two thirds of the way through a sentence when release is automatic unless the Parole Board intervenes'. Every use after that: 'statutory release'.

rewriting_guidance: Run this pass after the fix rounds of the verification loop and before its last check with rubric="full" on the assembled document. End it with humanizer_check_text and confirm prohibitions_clear is true, because cutting words can create or expose findings such as a comma splice or a new run-on.
Rule 3 is the one to spend time on in anything longer than a page. Read each paragraph and ask which words the sentence needs.
Do not apply the substitution lists as a find-and-replace. A long word chosen for rhythm at the end of a sentence can be the right word, and rule 6 covers it.
orwell.research_basis: Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' (1946). Added 2026-08-10 from the Day One case-study writing gate, which ran an Orwell layer by hand after this server's loop for the length of a 39-page document and kept catching the same three classes: stale figures, padding, and jargon substituted where a definition was wanted.

terms_of_art.description: Multi-word domain terms that contain a flagged word but have no plainer equivalent. A flagged word inside one of these is not reported, in any content type, because replacing it would change the claim (caveats.jargon_substitution_loses_meaning). Add a term only when every suggested alternative would make the sentence wrong, never to quiet a word that is merely common in a field.
terms_of_art.history: Added 2026-11-09 after a portfolio project excused 'differentiated instruction' by hand on every audit.
